name: World Vision US: international programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: World Vision US's spending abroad by region from its Form 990 Schedule F (Sub-Saharan Africa 71%, Central America and the Caribbean 11%, South America 5%, South Asia 4%, East Asia and the Pacific 3%, the Middle East 3%, the former Soviet states 2%), each region split equally over World Vision's main programme countries there (a judgment: no country split is published); the advocacy branch aims at the same people.
summary: World Vision US (World Vision, Inc.) spent $988 million on international programmes in its fiscal year to September 2025, almost all as grants to World Vision field offices (71% in Sub-Saharan Africa): child-sponsorship community development (health and nutrition, clean water, livelihoods, education) and food-crisis and disaster response, much of it WFP food and US government grants; plus $3.4 million of advocacy on global poverty. World Vision US publishes no outcome figures for its own spending, so each branch is built from its spending, judged costs per person and the research on that kind of work, and every branch is discounted for missing data. More than half of the result is relief (food and cash for some 15 million people at the partnership's $30 a person, valued over the months they cover, with a few excess crisis deaths averted), then child health and water, and livelihoods: because the relief reaches very poor people at a low cost per person. The biggest uncertainties are the missing-data discount, how much livelihoods work raises consumption, and the share of excess crisis deaths that food assistance averts.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: International programmes, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/world_vision.json) from World Vision US's Form 990: grants to World Vision field offices for child-sponsorship community development and relief, plus the US-side programme staff, travel and freight.

rows.label: Public awareness and education, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: World Vision US's advocacy to US officials and the public on global poverty, modelled as a branch below (it aims at the same people abroad as the international work).

rows.label: Spending on the modelled programmes, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: International programmes plus public awareness and education, without the donated goods and food commodities (they enter the credit shares, Convention 2): every programme line but the domestic one, which has its own model (world-vision-charityevals-domestic). Grants to World Vision field offices count as the work they fund.

rows.label: Total expenses without donated goods, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: World Vision US's total expenses less all donated goods and food commodities it passed on, at home and abroad.

rows.label: Programme expenses without donated goods, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: Programme expenses less the same donated goods and commodities.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: World Vision US's management ($58.7M) and fundraising ($143.0M) spread over its programmes in proportion to their cost: about 1.17. The field offices' own overheads are inside the grants and so inside program_spend.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled programmes, including overhead
rows.explainer: The spending above plus its share of management and fundraising.

rows.label: Share of international spending on relief and food-crisis response
rows.explainer: World Vision US doesn't split its international line. Anchors: the whole World Vision partnership spent $1,060M on relief and rehabilitation against $1,662M on development in fiscal 2025 (38.6% of programmes, Global Annual Report 2025, p. 22); World Vision US receives the partnership's US government and UN (mostly WFP food) grants, $511.8M (990 Part VIII line 1e, the same as the combined statements' $217.8M US government plus $294.0M other public grants), which are mostly food assistance and emergency response, while its private sponsorship money ($39 a month) funds development. So above the partnership's share: 45%, from 32% to 58%.

rows.label: Relief spending, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: International programmes times the relief share.

rows.label: World Vision partnership relief and rehabilitation spending, fiscal 2025

source.title: World Vision International, Global Annual Report 2025 (fiscal year to 30 September 2025)

rows.explainer: All World Vision entities' relief spending, the denominator of the cost per person reached below (subject to audit adjustment, the report says).

rows.label: People World Vision reached with humanitarian assistance, fiscal 2025

source.title: World Vision International, Global Annual Report 2025 (fiscal year to 30 September 2025)
source.quote: reach 35.6 million people affected by disaster with holistic humanitarian assistance

rows.explainer: World Vision's own count over its 104 emergency responses in 70 countries; 85% of food assistance was delivered in fragile contexts (same page). Counted people may overlap across responses: implementation_adj.

rows.label: Relief spending per person reached, partnership-wide
rows.explainer: About {{row:relief_cost_per_person}} a person: food rations, cash, water and other help for a few months.

rows.label: People reached by World Vision US's relief, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: World Vision US's relief spending at the partnership's cost per person reached: about 15 million people at the best guesses. World Vision US publishes no count of its own.

rows.label: Cost per person reached (relief)
rows.explainer: Context: the relief branch's full cost per person, overhead included.

rows.label: Donated goods shipped abroad (non-food), fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: Clothing, shoes, furniture, household fixtures, toys, school and medical supplies sent to field offices at US wholesale value (the shared figure): a goods branch of its own.

rows.label: Donated food commodities distributed abroad, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: US government and WFP food World Vision distributes, at the value on its books (the shared figure): part of the relief branch.

rows.label: Cash spent shipping and handing out the donated goods, per dollar of their value
rows.explainer: Ocean freight, customs, warehousing and distribution of donated goods, paid from the development budget; World Vision does not report it separately. 10% (3-30%) of the goods' recorded value.

rows.label: Cash spent on the donated goods
rows.explainer: The goods' recorded value times the handling cost per dollar.

rows.label: Development spending (child sponsorship and grants), fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: The rest of the international line less the donated goods shipped abroad and their handling: World Vision's area programmes funded by child sponsorship and grants (health and nutrition, water and sanitation, education, child protection, livelihoods, faith).

rows.label: Share of development spending on health and nutrition
rows.explainer: No sector split is published for World Vision US. Health and nutrition (community health workers, the timed-and-targeted counselling of mothers, malnutrition treatment, nets) is the largest sector of World Vision's area programmes in its annual report (pp. 8-9: 199,617 community health workers supported in 43 countries, 7.4 million children and mothers screened for malnutrition). Judgment 30% (20-40%).

rows.label: Share of development spending on water, sanitation and hygiene
rows.explainer: World Vision US funds most of the partnership's water work, much of it in Africa (2.8 million people given clean water in fiscal 2025, Global Annual Report p. 7). Judgment 25% (15-35%).

rows.label: Share of development spending on faith and church programmes
rows.explainer: Spiritual nurture of children and work with churches (6 million children, Global Annual Report 2024 p. 15) is part of every area programme; its cost stays in the model and it is given no value on the site's scale. Judgment 6% (2-12%).

rows.label: Of the remaining development spending, share on livelihoods
rows.explainer: The rest is livelihoods (savings groups, farming and land restoration, ultra-poor graduation) and education and child protection. World Vision reports 1.7 million savings-group members and 1.6 million hectares restored against 5.7 million children in education programmes (Global Annual Report 2025 pp. 9-12); livelihoods cost more per person. Judgment 55% (40-70%).

rows.label: Health and nutrition spending
rows.explainer: Health and nutrition spending.

rows.label: Cost per child covered by the health and nutrition package (birth to age five)
rows.explainer: Area programmes pay for community health workers' home visits in pregnancy and the first years (timed and targeted counselling), growth monitoring and treatment of malnutrition, nets and support to clinics. Anchors: community newborn-care packages in trials cost $10-50 per birth for the visits alone; with malnutrition treatment ($150-200 a child treated, about 1 in 20 children) and clinic support the package costs more. Judgment $150 (50-450) per child, the cohort of a year's births.

rows.label: Children covered by the health package
rows.explainer: Spending over the cost per child.

rows.label: Water, sanitation and hygiene spending
rows.explainer: Water, sanitation and hygiene spending.

rows.label: Cost per person given a new water supply (with sanitation and hygiene work)
rows.explainer: Anchored on the partnership's reach: World Vision gave 2.8 million people clean water in fiscal 2025 (Global Annual Report 2025, p. 8); World Vision US pays for about 30% of the partnership's development money (its development spending here against the partnership's $1,662M), so at its share of the reach about 0.85 million people, about $150 a person on this branch's spending: rural boreholes ($15-40 a person) plus piped schemes, school and clinic water, latrines and hygiene work. Lower if World Vision US funds more than its share of the water points, higher if it funds fewer. Judgment $150 ($75-250).

rows.label: People given a new water supply
rows.explainer: Spending over the cost per person.

rows.label: Livelihoods spending
rows.explainer: Livelihoods spending.

rows.label: Cost per household reached by livelihoods work (savings groups, farming, graduation)
rows.explainer: Anchored on the partnership's reach: 1.7 million savings-group members, about 700,000 families in farming and resilience work and 150,000 ultra-poor households (Global Annual Report 2025, p. 11), against World Vision US's share of the partnership's development money (about a third): about $180 a household, more than savings groups alone cost to form ($20-40 a member) because farming support, land restoration and graduation ($500-1,500 a household) are dearer. Judgment $180 ($110-400).

rows.label: Households reached by livelihoods work
rows.explainer: Households reached by livelihoods work.

rows.label: People per household (rural East and Southern Africa)
rows.explainer: The site's rural household sizes for three of World Vision's larger African programme countries, as the gains are shared by the household.

rows.label: Education and child protection spending
rows.explainer: Education and child protection spending.

rows.label: Cost per child reached by education programmes a year
rows.explainer: Reading clubs, teacher training, books and parents' groups (Unlock Literacy): $20-60 a child a year in World Vision's evaluations; child-protection work, school meals and early-childhood centres cost more. Judgment $100 ($30-300).

rows.label: Children reached by education programmes
rows.explainer: Children reached by education programmes.

rows.label: Death rate among the people reached during the crisis, without the response
rows.explainer: Most of the relief is food and cash assistance in fragile settings (85% of food assistance, Global Annual Report 2025 p. 16): Sudan, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia, the DRC, Afghanistan. Mortality surveys there commonly find crude death rates of 0.3-1 per 10,000 a day (0.011-0.037 a year); above 1 is the emergency threshold. Judgment 0.018 (0.012-0.035).

rows.label: Death rate in the same population before the crisis
rows.explainer: The site's crude death rates for three of the largest food-crisis responses (UN World Population Prospects), so only excess deaths count.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths the response averts among the people reached
rows.explainer: Food and cash in a food crisis prevent some deaths from hunger and the infections it worsens, but most people reached are not at risk of dying in the months covered and rations are often cut. The evidence is weak: the Cochrane review of cash in disasters (Pega et al. 2015) found one drought study with far fewer child deaths, all very low certainty; long-running cash programmes cut under-five deaths by about 8% (Richterman et al. 2023). Half the response is food assistance, the rest water, health, nutrition and protection. Judgment 10% (3-25%), higher than for cash relief in middle-income disasters because these are famine-risk settings.

rows.label: Years of the crisis the response covers per person
rows.explainer: About $30 a person buys one to three months of food rations or cash; some people get help all year, others one distribution. Judgment 0.2 years (0.1-0.4).

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Excess deaths over the time covered, times the share the response averts.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: A stand-in: the site's WHO Global Health Estimates split of diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa (facts/death_ages.json), used for excess crisis deaths, which are mostly hunger-worsened infections: {{row:share_under5}} under five, within the 40-60% the family's guidance gives for crises.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: From the same stand-in split (diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa, WHO GHE).

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: From the same stand-in split (diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa, WHO GHE); the rest valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: the illness averted by malnutrition treatment and emergency health care in some responses is in unmodelled benefits; the rations' value is counted below.

rows.label: Share of the relief cost reaching people as food, cash or goods at local value
rows.explainer: The rest is transport, storage, staff and monitoring; WFP food is valued at its procurement cost, often above local market prices. Judgment 65% (45-80%).

rows.label: Food, cash and goods delivered per person (US$)
rows.explainer: What each person gets, at local value: about {{row:value_delivered_per_person}}. The food's value is counted in full here as well as the deaths it averts, since the deaths averted are a small share of the people fed.

rows.label: Survey consumption per person, Kenya, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices.

rows.label: Survey consumption per person, Uganda, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: As for Kenya.

rows.label: Survey consumption per person, Malawi, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: As for Kenya.

rows.label: Survey consumption per person, Zambia, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: As for Kenya.

rows.label: Survey consumption per person, average of four African programme countries
rows.explainer: About $460 a year: the stand-in for the Sub-Saharan countries that get 71% of World Vision US's grants abroad (Schedule F).

rows.label: Price level of the stand-in countries against the US (market prices)
rows.explainer: The World Bank's ratio of consumption prices to US prices in the same four countries.

rows.label: Stand-in countries: food prices against all consumption prices (both relative to the US)
rows.explainer: The World Bank's International Comparison Program (2021), the same four countries.

rows.label: Crisis-affected people's consumption as a share of the stand-in average
rows.explainer: Food-insecure households in Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia or eastern DRC consume well under the national survey mean of the stable stand-ins; the poorest fifth in these surveys consume about 40% of the mean. Judgment 55% (35-80%).

rows.label: Consumption per person per year of the people reached (US$)
rows.explainer: Consumption per person per year of the people reached (US$).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person
rows.explainer: The relief on the site's one log-income scale over the time it is used: food, cash and goods raise consumption during the months each person is covered (years_exposed), so the gain is years_exposed × ln(1 + value ÷ the consumption of those months), the site's rule for a transfer used within a year.

rows.label: Neonatal mortality, Sub-Saharan Africa
rows.explainer: Deaths in the first 28 days per live birth, the rate the newborn package acts on (@sub_saharan_africa.neonatal_mortality_2023, UN IGME, 27 per 1,000); the range is the estimate's uncertainty and the spread across World Vision's countries.

rows.label: Deaths from one month to five years per live birth, Sub-Saharan Africa
rows.explainer: Under-five mortality less neonatal, Sub-Saharan Africa (@sub_saharan_africa.deaths_1_59m_per_birth_2023, UN IGME): 70 − 27 per 1,000.

rows.label: Stillbirths per birth, Sub-Saharan Africa
rows.explainer: Stillbirths per birth, Sub-Saharan Africa (@sub_saharan_africa.stillbirth_rate_2021, UN IGME, 21 per 1,000).

rows.label: Relative risk of neonatal death with community-based newborn packages
rows.explainer: The Cochrane review of community-based maternal and newborn packages (@newborn_care.community_package_neonatal_rr, 0.75, 0.67-0.83): home visits by community health workers and women's groups in pregnancy and after birth, World Vision's timed-and-targeted counselling model; the trials' effect, net of their control arms.

rows.label: Relative risk of stillbirth with community-based newborn packages
rows.explainer: The same review's effect on stillbirths (@newborn_care.community_package_stillbirth_rr, 0.81, 0.73-0.91).

rows.label: Reduction in deaths from one month to five years with the child health and nutrition work
rows.explainer: Community case management of malaria, pneumonia and diarrhoea, malnutrition treatment and nets can avert many child deaths in trials, but programme evaluations of community case management at scale mostly found no detectable fall in mortality (Amouzou et al. 2016, Malawi). Judgment 6% (0-15%).

rows.label: Child deaths averted per child covered
rows.explainer: Neonatal deaths (weighted to under-five-equivalents by the site's neonatal weight over its under-five one) plus later child deaths, per child covered; valued at the under-five weight below.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per child covered
rows.explainer: Stillbirths averted per child covered.

rows.label: Value of a child's death averted
rows.explainer: The site's under-five value of a death, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Value of a stillbirth averted
rows.explainer: The site's value of a stillbirth averted.

rows.label: Illness averted by the health work, as a share of its deaths' value
rows.explainer: The shared figure for health programmes abroad (@relief_development.health_programme_illness_value_ratio, {{row:health_morbidity_value_ratio}}, 0-30%): malnutrition, malaria and diarrhoea episodes averted and mothers' health, beside the deaths.

rows.label: Diarrhoeal deaths per person-year, Sub-Saharan Africa (all ages)
rows.explainer: The rate a new water supply acts on, Sub-Saharan Africa's (@sub_saharan_africa.diarrhoea_deaths_per_person_2021, GBD 2021, about 50 per 100,000, 30-80); wide because the estimate varies by country and year.

rows.label: Fall in diarrhoeal deaths from a new community water supply with hygiene work
rows.explainer: Meta-analyses of water interventions (Wolf et al. 2022, Lancet) find large falls in diarrhoea for piped water on premises and chlorination but small, uncertain ones for improved community sources such as boreholes, World Vision's main technology; chlorination trials cut child deaths more (Kremer et al. 2023). Judgment 12% (0-30%) of diarrhoeal deaths.

rows.label: Other deaths averted per diarrhoeal death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared ratio for water treatment: deaths from other causes that diarrhoea makes more likely.

rows.label: Years a new water point serves
rows.explainer: Hand pumps and boreholes last 10-15 years with repairs; piped schemes longer. Judgment 10 years (5-15).

rows.label: Share of those years the water point works
rows.explainer: About a quarter to a third of rural hand pumps in Sub-Saharan Africa are broken at any time (Rural Water Supply Network); World Vision's own sustainability studies find most of its points working. Judgment 70% (50-85%).

rows.label: Working years of the water point, discounted
rows.explainer: Each year's benefit at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Value of a diarrhoeal death averted
rows.explainer: The site's age split of diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa (facts/death_ages.json, WHO GHE) by the site's values by age.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person given water (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Deaths averted per person given water (before adjustments).

rows.label: Value of water-fetching time saved, as a share of consumption
rows.explainer: The shared figure for time saved fetching water, mostly women's and girls' (@water.time_saved_consumption_share, {{row:wash_time_saved_share}} of consumption, 0-3%).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person from time saved, over the water point's life
rows.explainer: ln(consumption) gain per person from time saved, over the water point's life.

rows.label: Consumption gain for a household reached by livelihoods work
rows.explainer: Savings-group trials find small or no consumption gains (Beaman et al. 2014 Mali; Ksoll et al. 2016 Malawi: more meals; Gash 2017 review); farming support and land restoration a few percent; graduation programmes 5-10% for the few reached. Judgment 1.5% (0-5%).

rows.label: Years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared figure for livelihood programmes abroad (@relief_development.livelihood_gain_years, 2 years, 1-4): World Vision's savings groups often keep meeting; farming gains fade without support.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted
rows.explainer: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted.

rows.label: Deaths averted by higher incomes, as a share of the consumption benefits
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/aid_value.json), times your value of a life, for the livelihood branch.

rows.label: Learning gain per child reached (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: World Vision's reading clubs and teacher training: its own reports show more children reading with comprehension (53% against 35% of non-participants, Global Annual Report 2025 p. 9), uncontrolled; trials of similar literacy programmes find 0.05-0.2 SD. Judgment 0.08 SD (0.02-0.2).

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of skill still there in adult life
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.earnings_gain_per_sd_adult_skills_lmic: 20%, 10% to 30%), from the Center for Global Development's review of the studies linking adults' reading and maths to their earnings, per SD of skill still there in adult life.

rows.label: Share of the learning gain that lasts into adulthood
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (@education.test_gain_persistence_to_adulthood: {{row:education_persistence}}, 20% to 70%): test-score gains fade, a fifth to a half of a year's learning carrying into the next grade in Pakistan's schools (Andrabi and others 2011).

rows.label: Years from the programme to adult work
rows.explainer: The shared figure for primary-age education abroad (@education.years_primary_programme_to_work, 10 years, 6-15): the children World Vision's education work reaches are mostly 6-12 years old.

rows.label: Working years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared figure for later-life income gains.

rows.label: Household members sharing the earnings gain
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared figure.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per child reached, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + education_learning_gain_sd * education_earnings_per_sd * education_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - education_years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × earnings per SD × persistence) for each working year, discounted, after the wait to adult work, shared with the household.

rows.label: US foreign aid kept or added per dollar of advocacy, credited to World Vision
rows.explainer: World Vision US is one of hundreds of groups lobbying for the US aid budget, which fell sharply in 2025 regardless (USAID closed, a $9 billion rescission). Its share of what advocacy keeps is small; studies of organised constituent contact find votes move but budgets rarely. Judgment $0.50 of aid per dollar (0-5).

rows.label: Value of a dollar of US aid, as a multiple of cash to the poor
rows.explainer: The site's shared value of a dollar of a rich country's aid budget whose use isn't known more exactly (facts/aid_value.json): about {{row:aid_value_vs_cash}} @cash.uov_per_dollar (0.4-2×), a mix of global health aid at GiveWell's Global Fund and Gavi figures, humanitarian aid at a fifth of cash and other development aid at about half. The same figure in every model that values aid won or kept.

rows.label: Donated goods per person who gets them (US wholesale value)
rows.explainer: A few items of clothing, shoes or household goods per person in a distribution; furniture and fixtures go to schools and clinics. Judgment $30 ($10-80).

rows.label: People who get donated goods
rows.explainer: People who get donated goods.

rows.label: What the goods are worth to the people who get them, as a share of their US wholesale value
rows.explainer: US wholesale value is far above what the same goods cost in a local market in Africa or Central America (second-hand clothing sells for a fraction), and people can't choose what they get. Judgment 45% (25-75%), below the domestic model's 60% for goods given in the US.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person from the goods
rows.explainer: At the stand-in countries' average consumption, the people in World Vision's area programmes.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, relief deaths averted
rows.explainer: Applies to the deaths averted (and illness) only: they rest on weak evidence, already wide in share_excess_averted, and the studies are of other settings. The goods' value is their cost, which needs no effect study, so it isn't discounted here. 0.85 (0.7-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, relief
rows.explainer: The question is whether the people reached would have been fed or helped anyway, not who delivers. UN humanitarian appeals were well under half funded in 2025 after the US cuts, and food pipelines in Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and the DRC were cut to part rations, so another agency would rarely have filled the gap; but World Vision's WFP food would partly have gone through another partner to the same people. 70% (45-90%).

rows.label: World Vision's share of the resources behind the deaths averted, relief
rows.explainer: WFP's own costs for in-kind food add 15-30% beyond the commodities, and communities' volunteers help with distributions. World Vision's and the commodities' share of all the resources behind the food reaching people: 85% (70-100%).

rows.label: World Vision's share of the resources behind the relief goods' value
rows.explainer: The goods are valued at a share of the relief resources (relief_goods_value_share), so WFP's off-book shipping and storage don't enter the value counted; only communities' volunteers and local partners delivering it do. 95% (85-100%).

rows.label: Relief: World Vision's own spending
rows.explainer: Relief spending less the donated food commodities.

rows.label: Donated food commodities at local market prices
rows.explainer: The commodities at their recorded US value, at retail, at the local food price level.

rows.label: Relief: World Vision's own spending against the donated commodities
rows.explainer: Convention 2: the donated commodities are not in the cost, so World Vision gets its own spending's share of the food's resources.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, health
rows.explainer: The newborn effect comes from trials of intensive packages under study conditions; World Vision's version runs at scale through community health workers with variable quality and no published mortality evaluation. 0.5 (0.3-0.8).

rows.label: Counterfactual, health
rows.explainer: Governments and other NGOs run some of the same services where World Vision works. 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: World Vision's share of the resources, health
rows.explainer: Community health workers are often government-paid or volunteers and the clinics are the government's; World Vision's spending is part of the resources. 60% (40-80%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, wash
rows.explainer: The reduction is already a judgment on community sources; external validity to World Vision's sites: 0.75 (0.5-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, wash
rows.explainer: Some communities would have got a water point from the government or another NGO within a few years. 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: World Vision's share of the resources, wash
rows.explainer: Communities contribute labour and materials and pay for repairs; local governments maintain some schemes. 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, livelihood
rows.explainer: The gain is already set at the low end of the trials; 0.8 (0.5-1) for self-selection of members.

rows.label: Counterfactual, livelihood
rows.explainer: The households are chosen as among the poorest in World Vision's areas, where few other savings, farming or graduation programmes run, and the gain is measured against comparison households that mostly got none; some would have joined a group formed by another NGO or the government's extension service. 90%, from 70% (other programmes common, as in parts of Kenya and Uganda) to 100% (none).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, gik
rows.explainer: 1: the goods are valued at a judged share of their recorded value, which needs no effect study; the doubt about what they are worth to the people who get them is in gik_inkind_equivalence.

rows.label: Counterfactual, gik
rows.explainer: Some of the goods would have reached the same people through another charity or the second-hand market at a lower price. 75% (50-95%).

rows.label: Donated goods abroad at local market prices
rows.explainer: The goods at the donors' wholesale value, at US market value (the shared ratio), at the local price level.

rows.label: Donated goods: World Vision's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Convention 2: World Vision's handling cost over that plus the goods at local prices.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, education
rows.explainer: Learning gain and its link to earnings rest on other programmes' trials. 0.6 (0.3-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, education
rows.explainer: Schools exist anyway; the programme adds to them, as the effect assumes. 90% (60-100%).

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (relief_dalys_unadjusted * (relief_deaths_share_unadj * relief_attribution_share + (1 - relief_deaths_share_unadj) * relief_goods_attribution_share) * relief_commodities_credit_share + health_dalys_unadjusted * health_attribution_share + wash_dalys_unadjusted * wash_attribution_share + livelihood_dalys_unadjusted + education_dalys_unadjusted + gik_dalys_unadjusted * gik_attribution_share + awareness_dalys_unadjusted) / (relief_dalys_unadjusted + health_dalys_unadjusted + wash_dalys_unadjusted + livelihood_dalys_unadjusted + education_dalys_unadjusted + gik_dalys_unadjusted * gik_attribution_share + awareness_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: relief, health and water share credit with WFP, governments and communities (their own rows), relief and the goods also with the donated commodities and goods; livelihoods and education are World Vision's own spending, so 1.

rows.label: Share of credit used: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only (the health and water branches apply their own rows, health_attribution_share and wash_attribution_share); it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: Every count and share here is World Vision's own or a judgment from its spending; aid diverted, double-counted people and programmes delivered below design. World Vision is audited by KPMG and its US government grants by the single audit (no major findings in fiscal 2025, Schedule of Findings). 85% (70-95%), for every branch.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Sponsorship money is fungible across a field office's programmes, and other support offices may give less where World Vision US gives more (below 1); its grants sometimes draw in matching public money (above 1). 1 (0.9-1.05).

rows.label: Years between a gift and its spending abroad
rows.explainer: Unspent funds over a year's spending, as the template's recipe: the combined statements hold $354.8M received for relief and development and $224.3M of restricted relief, development and sponsorship funds (note 13), against $2.2 billion of international programme spending a year: about 0.25 years; sponsorship gifts go monthly. Judgment 0.3 years (0.15-0.6).

rows.label: Years from the field office's spending to the benefit
rows.explainer: Relief goes out in weeks; water points and health work take months to start. Judgment 0.4 years (0.1-1).

rows.label: Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The waits at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Missing-data discount, relief
rows.explainer: Thin: World Vision US publishes no count of the people its relief reached; reach is its spending at the partnership's cost per person and the deaths averted rest on the research on food and cash in crises. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, health
rows.explainer: Thin: the children covered are spending over a judged cost per child, and the effect comes from trials of community newborn packages, not an evaluation of World Vision's. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, wash
rows.explainer: Thin: people given water are spending over a judged cost per person, and the effect is a judgment from meta-analyses of other water programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, livelihood
rows.explainer: Thin: households reached are spending over a judged cost, the gain from other programmes' trials. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, education
rows.explainer: Thin: children reached are spending over a judged cost; the learning gain is World Vision's uncontrolled monitoring and other programmes' trials. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, gik
rows.explainer: Thin: World Vision US publishes no count of the people its goods abroad reach; reach and value are judgments. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, awareness
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome data; the aid kept is a judgment. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments, relief deaths averted
rows.formula: relief_evidence_adj * relief_counterfactual_adj * relief_attribution_share * relief_commodities_credit_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * relief_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments to the deaths averted (and the illness counted directly).

rows.formula: relief_counterfactual_adj * relief_goods_attribution_share * relief_commodities_credit_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * relief_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: All adjustments to the goods' value: no evidence step (goods valued at a share of their cost need no effect study).

rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: All adjustments, gik

rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: All adjustments, awareness
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments. The aid kept is already World Vision's credited marginal effect, so no other adjustment applies.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (relief_dalys_unadjusted * (relief_deaths_share_unadj * relief_evidence_adj + (1 - relief_deaths_share_unadj)) + health_dalys_unadjusted * health_evidence_adj + wash_dalys_unadjusted * wash_evidence_adj + livelihood_dalys_unadjusted * livelihood_evidence_adj + education_dalys_unadjusted * education_evidence_adj + gik_dalys_unadjusted * gik_evidence_adj + awareness_dalys_unadjusted) / (relief_dalys_unadjusted + health_dalys_unadjusted + wash_dalys_unadjusted + livelihood_dalys_unadjusted + education_dalys_unadjusted + gik_dalys_unadjusted + awareness_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row; awareness has none (1).

rows.label: Counterfactual: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (relief_dalys_unadjusted * relief_counterfactual_adj + health_dalys_unadjusted * health_counterfactual_adj + wash_dalys_unadjusted * wash_counterfactual_adj + livelihood_dalys_unadjusted * livelihood_counterfactual_adj + education_dalys_unadjusted * education_counterfactual_adj + gik_dalys_unadjusted * gik_counterfactual_adj + awareness_dalys_unadjusted) / (relief_dalys_unadjusted + health_dalys_unadjusted + wash_dalys_unadjusted + livelihood_dalys_unadjusted + education_dalys_unadjusted + gik_dalys_unadjusted + awareness_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only; awareness has none (1).

rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: every branch is thin.

rows.label: All adjustments combined: outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (relief_dalys + health_dalys + wash_dalys + livelihood_dalys + education_dalys + gik_dalys + awareness_dalys) / (relief_dalys_unadjusted + health_dalys_unadjusted + wash_dalys_unadjusted + livelihood_dalys_unadjusted + education_dalys_unadjusted + gik_dalys_unadjusted + awareness_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own total, weighted by its outcome before adjustments in healthy years.

rows.label: Unmodelled: sanitation's and hygiene's own health effects
rows.explainer: Latrines and handwashing come with the water work and cut diarrhoea beyond the water itself (Wolf et al. 2022); the water branch is about a tenth of the result, so about a quarter to a half of it again: +2.5% (0 to +6%).

rows.label: Unmodelled: women's empowerment and resilience from savings groups
rows.explainer: Savings-group trials find gains in women's say in household decisions and in coping with shocks, not valued in consumption: +1% (0 to +3%) of the result.

rows.label: Unmodelled: food aid's harm to local farmers' prices
rows.explainer: Imported food rations can lower local grain prices for farmers near distributions; most of the relief is in deficit areas where the effect is small: -1% (-3% to 0).

rows.label: Unmodelled: aid dependency and displaced local initiative
rows.explainer: Long-running area programmes (15 years and more) may crowd out local government services or community self-help: -1% (-3% to 0).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The signed items above, each sized against the branch it belongs to. Child protection is already bought inside the education branch's spending, faith work is given no value through faith_share, and funging is in leverage_funging_adj, so none is counted here again.
